youtube_title: Could a Rare Bible Beat a Debt Collector in New York? 🦝⚖️
caption: New York's CPLR 5205 lists religious texts used by a debtor's family as exempt without a stated dollar cap, while other books are capped at $500. A textual quirk — not a tested strategy.
script: In New York, you could owe someone a fortune, and they still might not be able to touch your million dollar Bible. [disclaimer] In New York, the wording of the law makes that a real question! Here's how it works. If you lose a lawsuit and owe money, the winner can go after your stuff. But New York says some stuff is off limits. They can't take everything. Cash and bank accounts? Only a small amount is protected. Ordinary books? Up to five hundred dollars' worth. Okay, normal. But then, right in that same line, the law lists religious books, family pictures, and school books. And for those? It doesn't give a dollar limit at all. None! So on paper, the family Bible sits in its own protected group. Which makes you wonder. What if that Bible is a super rare antique worth a fortune? Here's the honest answer. Nobody has proven this works in court. It's just a weird gap in the wording. And there are big catches. The book has to actually be used by you or your family. It doesn't count if the debt is for the book itself. And if you dump your money into a fancy Bible just to hide it from the people you owe, you can run into fraud rules and bankruptcy rules. That's a whole new problem! [loop] So before you go shopping for the world's most expensive Bible, remember
